title: Arrays (fixed-length sequences) and a Span preview
hook: An array is a fixed-size list of items stored in one block of memory. You pick the size when you create it, and it never grows — that is the first collection type every C# program uses.

blocks.text: An array in C# is written as int[] scores or string[] names. It has a Length property that never changes after creation. You access items with an index: scores[0] is the first element. Arrays live on the heap (they are reference types), even though the items inside might be value types like int. A Simple Queue Service (SQS) batch of exactly 10 messages maps naturally to an array — you know the size when the receive call returns.

entries.plainDefinition: A fixed-length, zero-based collection where every slot is the same type.
entries.example: int[] scores = new int[3]; creates three int slots.

entries.plainDefinition: The number of slots in the array. Set once at creation; cannot grow.
entries.example: scores.Length is 3 forever for the array above.

entries.plainDefinition: A lightweight view over a slice of memory — an array, stack buffer, or other storage — without copying the data.
entries.example: Span<char> slice = line.AsSpan(0, 10); reads the first 10 characters.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET runtime that loads your compiled code and manages memory.
entries.example: When you run dotnet run, the CLR executes your program.

blocks.text: Arrays are the fastest way to store a known number of items with constant-time indexing. They are also the foundation every other collection builds on — List<T> is literally an array plus a count. Picking an array when you need a growable buffer leads to painful resize logic; picking a List when the size is fixed wastes memory and hides intent. Understanding array covariance (a subtle trap) also sets you up for why generics exist in module 09.

blocks.title: Fixed size is a feature
blocks.body: If the batch size is capped — SQS returns at most 10 messages — an array matches reality. If you need to append later, use List<T> instead.

sections.heading: How arrays work step by step

items.title: Declare the type and size
items.body: int[] scores = new int[3]; allocates a heap object with three int slots, all initialized to 0.

items.title: Write values by index
items.body: scores[0] = 95; sets the first slot. Indices run from 0 to Length - 1.

items.title: Read values by index
items.body: int top = scores[0]; is O(1) — the runtime computes the memory address directly.

items.title: Stay inside bounds
items.body: scores[3] throws IndexOutOfRangeException. The runtime checks every access.

snippet.label: Fixed batch as array
snippet.explanation: Once the receive call returns, the batch is a closed set. An array matches that shape. A retry is a new receive and a new array.

snippet.label: Jagged versus rectangular arrays
snippet.explanation: int[][] is an array where each row can have a different length. int[,] is a single rectangular block. They are different types — you cannot assign one to the other.

snippet.label: Array covariance trap
snippet.explanation: The compiler allows assigning string[] to object[] because arrays are covariant. Writing an int into a string slot fails at run time, not compile time. List<string> does not allow this — that is why generics exist.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling Add on an array typed as IList<T> throws NotSupportedException — arrays do not grow. Using object[] as a mixed-type bag and hitting array covariance bugs. Trying to store Span<T> as a class field — Span is a ref struct and cannot live on the heap; full rules are in module 17.

interviewTakeaways: Arrays have fixed Length; indexing is O(1); they are reference types on the heap.
Array covariance (string[] to object[]) can throw ArrayTypeMismatchException at run time.
Span<T> is a zero-copy view over memory — full treatment is module 17.
commonPitfalls: Calling Add on an array typed as IList<T> and being surprised by NotSupportedException.
Using object[] as a heterogeneous bag and hitting array covariance bugs.
Trying to store Span<T> on a worker class field — illegal; wait for module 17 to see why.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript arrays grow with push(). C# arrays do not. A JS Array is closer to List<T> than to T[].

jsTsCorrelations.concept: T[] vs readonly T[] vs tuple
jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript T[] is a growable JS array at run time. C# T[] is fixed. TS tuples are closer in intent to a fixed array but still JS arrays underneath.
